questions.enonce_markdown:
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes according to the equation

$2\mathrm{H_2O_2(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}$

The reaction is first order with respect to hydrogen peroxide and is catalyzed by manganese (IV) oxide

(i) Sketch in the space below, the change in concentration (y-axis) of hydrogen peroxide with time (x-axis)

(ii) Define

A: Order of reaction

B: Catalyst *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Sketch.** For a first-order reaction the rate is proportional to the concentration, $-\dfrac{d[\mathrm{H_2O_2}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{H_2O_2}]$, so the concentration decays **exponentially**: $[\mathrm{H_2O_2}] = [\mathrm{H_2O_2}]_0\,e^{-kt}$.

The sketch to draw:

- axes: **time** on the x-axis, **[H$_2$O$_2$] / mol dm$^{-3}$** on the y-axis;
- the curve starts on the y-axis at the initial concentration $[\mathrm{H_2O_2}]_0$ and falls steeply at first;
- the gradient (the rate) becomes smaller and smaller as the concentration falls: the curve is **concave up** and gets closer and closer to the time axis (asymptote) without ever reaching zero;
- the **half-life is constant**: the concentration halves in each successive equal interval of time.

| time | 0 | $t_{1/2}$ | $2t_{1/2}$ | $3t_{1/2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $[\mathrm{H_2O_2}]$ | $[\;]_0$ | $\tfrac{1}{2}[\;]_0$ | $\tfrac{1}{4}[\;]_0$ | $\tfrac{1}{8}[\;]_0$ |

(The $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ catalyst only increases $k$, so the curve is steeper than for the uncatalysed reaction, but it keeps the same exponential shape.)

**(ii) Definitions.**

**A: Order of reaction.** The order with respect to a reactant is the **power to which the concentration of that reactant is raised in the experimentally determined rate equation**; it shows how the rate depends on that concentration (for example, rate $= k[\mathrm{H_2O_2}]^1$ is first order). The overall order is the sum of the individual orders.

**B: Catalyst.** A catalyst is a substance that **increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy**, and which is **not used up** (it is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction).

questions.enonce_markdown: State two postulates of collision theory. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any two of the following postulates of collision theory:

1. Particles (atoms, molecules or ions) must **collide** with one another for a reaction to occur; the rate of reaction depends on the frequency of collisions.
2. Only collisions in which the particles have a **combined kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy**, $E_a$, are effective (result in reaction); most collisions are not.
3. The colliding particles must be in the **correct orientation** (the reacting parts of the molecules must meet) for a collision to be effective.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What is the Born-Haber cycle?

(ii) Below is the Born-Haber cycle for the formation of sodium chloride, NaCl.

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2022-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

Label the energy changes represented by $\Delta H_1$, $\Delta H_4$ and $\Delta H_6$.

(iii) Explain, in terms of enthalpy changes, why some arrows are pointing upwards while some are pointing downwards. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The Born-Haber cycle** is an **enthalpy (energy) cycle based on Hess's law** that links the **lattice enthalpy of an ionic compound** to its **standard enthalpy of formation** and to other enthalpy changes that can be measured (atomisation, ionisation energy, electron affinity). The lattice enthalpy cannot be measured directly, so it is calculated from the cycle.

**(ii) Labels** (the figure shows the levels $\mathrm{Na(s)} + \tfrac12\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}$, $\mathrm{Na(g)} + \tfrac12\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}$, $\mathrm{Na(g)} + \mathrm{Cl(g)}$, $\mathrm{Na^+(g)} + \mathrm{Cl(g)} + e^-$, $\mathrm{Na^+(g)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(g)}$ and $\mathrm{NaCl(s)}$):

- $\Delta H_1$: **standard enthalpy of formation of sodium chloride**, $\mathrm{Na(s)} + \tfrac12\mathrm{Cl_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(s)}$ (downward arrow from the elements to the solid).
- $\Delta H_4$: **first ionisation energy of sodium**, $\mathrm{Na(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^+(g)} + e^-$.
- $\Delta H_6$: **lattice enthalpy of formation** of NaCl (enthalpy change when one mole of solid NaCl is formed from its gaseous ions), $\mathrm{Na^+(g)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(s)}$. (If lattice enthalpy is defined for the opposite process, breaking the lattice, its value is the same with the opposite sign.)

For completeness: $\Delta H_2$ is the enthalpy of atomisation (sublimation) of sodium, $\Delta H_3$ the enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine ($\tfrac12$ the Cl-Cl bond enthalpy) and $\Delta H_5$ the first electron affinity of chlorine. By Hess's law, $\Delta H_1 = \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3 + \Delta H_4 + \Delta H_5 + \Delta H_6$.

**(iii) Direction of the arrows.** In an enthalpy-level diagram, an **upward arrow means the enthalpy of the system increases: energy is absorbed from the surroundings, the step is endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$)**. This is the case for atomisation of sodium ($\Delta H_2$), atomisation of chlorine ($\Delta H_3$) and ionisation of sodium ($\Delta H_4$): energy is needed to break metallic bonds or the Cl-Cl bond, or to remove an electron against the attraction of the nucleus.

A **downward arrow means the enthalpy of the system decreases: energy is released to the surroundings, the step is exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$)**. This is the case when the chlorine atom gains an electron ($\Delta H_5$, electron affinity), when the oppositely charged ions come together to form the lattice ($\Delta H_6$, strong electrostatic attraction) and for the overall formation of NaCl from its elements ($\Delta H_1$).

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the x-ray power pattern of KCl shows a cone at $\theta = 13.98$ and the distance between successive layers is $6.73\times10^{-9}$ cm. Use the Bragg's equation to calculate the wavelength of the x-rays. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Bragg's equation:** $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$, where $d$ is the distance between successive layers (planes) of atoms and $\theta$ the angle of the diffracted cone. For the first-order reflection, $n = 1$; $\theta = 13.98^\circ$ (the degree sign is missing in the question) and $d = 6.73\times10^{-9}$ cm.

$$\lambda = \frac{2d\sin\theta}{n} = 2 \times 6.73\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm} \times \sin 13.98^\circ = 2 \times 6.73\times10^{-9} \times 0.2416$$

$$\boxed{\lambda \approx 3.25\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm}}\quad (= 3.25\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.0325\ \mathrm{nm})$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Covalent bonds, ionic bonds and intermolecular forces are building forces in substances.

(i) Define

A: Covalent bond

B: Ionic bond

(ii) Identify the types of intermolecular forces in each of the following substances

| Substance | Intermolecular force |
|---|---|
| Ice | |
| Propanone | |
| Kerosene | |

*[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Definitions.**

**A: Covalent bond.** A covalent bond is the **strong electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the two positively charged nuclei** of the bonded atoms. It forms when two atoms (usually non-metals) share a pair of electrons.

**B: Ionic bond.** An ionic bond is the **strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions**, formed when a metal atom transfers one or more electrons to a non-metal atom (for example $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ in NaCl).

**(ii) Intermolecular forces.**

| Substance | Intermolecular force |
|---|---|
| Ice | **Hydrogen bonding** (between $\mathrm{H}$ of one water molecule and a lone pair on the $\mathrm{O}$ of a neighbour), together with London dispersion forces |
| Propanone | **Permanent dipole - permanent dipole attractions** (the C=O bond is polar), together with London dispersion forces; no hydrogen bonding because no H is bonded to O, N or F |
| Kerosene | **London (instantaneous dipole - induced dipole, van der Waals) dispersion forces** only, since the hydrocarbon molecules are non-polar |

questions.enonce_markdown:
For the reaction: $2\mathrm{NO(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{N_2(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$

The following data was obtained at the same temperature.

| Experiment | $[\mathrm{NO}]$ / mol dm$^{-3}$ | $[\mathrm{H_2}]$ / mol dm$^{-3}$ | Initial rate / mol dm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.30 | 0.15 | $1.4\times10^{-4}$ |
| 2 | 0.60 | 0.15 | $5.6\times10^{-4}$ |
| 3 | 0.60 | 0.30 | $1.12\times10^{-3}$ |
| 4 | 0.30 | 0.30 | $2.8\times10^{-4}$ |

Deduce

(i) The order of the reaction with respect to NO and $\mathrm{H_2}$.

(ii) The overall order of the reaction *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Orders.** Change one concentration at a time.

*Order with respect to NO* (experiments 1 and 2: $[\mathrm{H_2}]$ constant at 0.15, $[\mathrm{NO}]$ doubled from 0.30 to 0.60):

$$\frac{\text{rate}_2}{\text{rate}_1} = \frac{5.6\times10^{-4}}{1.4\times10^{-4}} = 4 = 2^m \Rightarrow m = 2$$

The reaction is **second order with respect to NO** (doubling $[\mathrm{NO}]$ multiplies the rate by 4).

*Order with respect to $\mathrm{H_2}$* (experiments 2 and 3: $[\mathrm{NO}]$ constant at 0.60, $[\mathrm{H_2}]$ doubled from 0.15 to 0.30):

$$\frac{\text{rate}_3}{\text{rate}_2} = \frac{1.12\times10^{-3}}{5.6\times10^{-4}} = 2 = 2^n \Rightarrow n = 1$$

The reaction is **first order with respect to $\mathrm{H_2}$**. (Check with experiments 1 and 4: $[\mathrm{H_2}]$ doubled at constant $[\mathrm{NO}]$ gives $2.8\times10^{-4}/1.4\times10^{-4} = 2$, in agreement.)

**(ii) Overall order** $= 2 + 1 = \mathbf{3}$ (third order). Rate equation: $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{H_2}]$, with $k = \dfrac{1.4\times10^{-4}}{(0.30)^2(0.15)} = 1.04\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol^{-2}\,dm^{6}\,s^{-1}}$ (the same value is obtained from each experiment).
